button.name: button
button.title: Button
button.description: A button for actions. CSS component with one class and no JavaScript.
button.intro: The class goes on an ordinary `<button>`. No JavaScript is loaded, and it works the same in every framework.
button.code:
<button class="lt-button">Send application</button>
<button class="lt-button" data-variant="secondary">Save draft</button>
<button class="lt-button" data-variant="ghost">Add attachment</button>
<button class="lt-button" data-variant="danger">Delete application</button>

demo.html:
<button class="lt-button">Send application</button>
<button class="lt-button" data-variant="secondary">Save draft</button>
<button class="lt-button" data-variant="ghost">Add attachment</button>
<button class="lt-button" data-variant="danger">Delete application</button>

alert.name: alert
alert.title: Alert
alert.description: A message about the whole page or the whole form. CSS component with two classes and no JavaScript.
alert.intro: A box that says something about the whole: that the application was sent, that the service is down, that the deadline is approaching. If the message is about one field, it belongs under the field as an [Error Text](../error-text/) or a [Help Text](../help-text/).
alert.code:
Your case has been registered

You will get a reply within three weeks.

We have updated the service. You need to sign in again.

Your application has been sent. A receipt is on its way to your email.

The application deadline is in three days.

Your application was not sent

The network did not respond. Try again in a moment.

demo.html:
Your case has been registered

You will get a reply within three weeks.

We have updated the service. You need to sign in again.

Your application has been sent. A receipt is on its way to your email.

The application deadline is in three days.

Your application was not sent

The network did not respond. Try again in a moment.

tag.name: tag
tag.title: Tag
tag.description: A tag for topics and filters. A CSS component with one class and no JavaScript.
tag.intro: A tag labels content: topics on an article, chosen filters above a list. If the tag says what state something is in, such as "Approved" or "Overdue", [Badge](../badge/) is the right choice instead.
tag.code: Housing benefit Nursery Archived

demo.html: Housing benefit Nursery Archived

badge.name: badge
badge.title: Badge
badge.description: Compact status badge. A CSS component with one class and no JavaScript.
badge.intro: A small badge that shows what state something is in. The colour is set with `data-color`.
badge.code: In progress Approved Attachment missing Rejected Archived

demo.html: In progress Approved Attachment missing Rejected Archived

switch.name: switch
switch.title: Switch
switch.description: A switch for a setting that takes effect immediately. CSS component with two classes and no JavaScript.
switch.intro: A checkbox with `role="switch"`. Screen readers then say "on" and "off" instead of "checked", while the keyboard and `FormData` work as for an ordinary checkbox.

spinner.name: spinner
spinner.title: Spinner
spinner.description: A wait indicator for something in progress. CSS component with one class and no JavaScript.
spinner.intro: A ring that spins while something loads. If you know how long it takes, or how far it has got, [Progress](../progress/) is better. This one only says that something is in progress.

breadcrumbs.name: breadcrumbs
breadcrumbs.title: Breadcrumbs
breadcrumbs.description: A breadcrumb trail that shows where on the site the user is. A CSS component with one class and no JavaScript.
breadcrumbs.intro: The path from the front page to where the user is now. The class goes on an `<ol>` inside a `<nav>`: the order matters, so the list has to be numbered even though the numbers are not shown.
breadcrumbs.code:
1. Home
  2. My cases
  3. Application 2026-0481

demo.html:
1. Home
  2. My cases
  3. Application 2026-0481

progress.name: progress
progress.title: Progress
progress.description: A progress bar for something that has an end. CSS component with one class and no JavaScript.
progress.intro: The class goes on a real `<progress>`. The element has the semantics built in: the browser reports it as `role="progressbar"` and announces how far it has got, so you write neither a role, `aria-valuenow` nor `aria-valuemax`. If you build the bar from `<div>` elements, you have to write all of that yourself, and keep it in step with the number.
progress.code:
<progress class="lt-progress" value="3" max="7"
          aria-label="Application progress" aria-valuetext="Step 3 of 7"></progress>

<progress class="lt-progress" value="100" max="100" data-color="success"
          aria-label="Upload complete"></progress>

<progress class="lt-progress" aria-label="Fetching your applications"></progress>

demo.html:
<progress class="lt-progress" value="3" max="7"
          aria-label="Application progress" aria-valuetext="Step 3 of 7"></progress>

<progress class="lt-progress" value="100" max="100" data-color="success"
          aria-label="Upload complete"></progress>

<progress class="lt-progress" aria-label="Fetching your applications"></progress>

toast.name: toast
toast.title: Toast
toast.description: A queue of short messages in the corner of the screen. Standalone component.
toast.intro: The element is the container, not the message. You add it once in the app and call `show()` when there is something to report.
toast.code:
<lt-toast id="messages" class="lt-toast" role="status" aria-live="polite"
          aria-atomic="false"
          aria-label="Messages" data-ignore-morph></lt-toast>

<button class="lt-button" id="save" type="button">Save application</button>

demo.html: <button class="lt-button" id="demo-toast-button" type="button">Save the application</button> <lt-toast id="demo-toast-queue" label="Notifications"></lt-toast>

skeleton.name: skeleton
skeleton.title: Skeleton
skeleton.description: A placeholder that shows the shape of content being loaded. A CSS component with one class and no JavaScript.
skeleton.intro: Grey shapes that show where the content will appear. They are always hidden from screen readers, so the wait has to be announced somewhere as well. If there is no shape to show, or the wait is short, [Spinner](../spinner/) is simpler.

connection-status.name: connection-status
connection-status.title: Connection Status
connection-status.description: Tells the user when the connection to the server is gone. Standalone component.
connection-status.intro: A page that loses its connection looks completely normal, but is frozen. If the user fills in a form over a dead connection, everything is gone when she presses send.

dialog.name: dialog
dialog.title: Dialog
dialog.description: Modal dialog built on the native dialog element. Six classes and no JavaScript, with an optional component for servers that cannot call showModal().
dialog.intro: The class goes on a `<dialog>`, and the rest is the browser's own element. If your app runs JavaScript in the browser, you need nothing from LO-TEK: open the dialog with `showModal()` and close it with `close()`.
dialog.code:
Delete the application?

The application and its attachments will be gone. This cannot be undone.

demo.html:
Delete the application?

This cannot be undone

The application and its attachments will be gone. This cannot be undone.

tabs.name: tabs
tabs.title: Tabs
tabs.description: Tab list of links to their panels. Frame component.
tabs.intro: The tabs are links to their panels. Without JavaScript the row is a table of contents, and the panels follow one after another below it. With JavaScript the component turns the links into tabs: Tab skips past the whole row and into the selected panel, the arrow keys move between the tabs, and the screen reader says "tab, 2 of 3, selected" where it would otherwise have said "link".
tabs.code:

card.name: card
card.title: Card
card.description: A box that groups content that belongs together. A CSS component with two classes and no JavaScript.
card.intro: A frame around content that belongs together, such as one case in a list of cases. The card is a container, not a component with behaviour: the content decides what the user can do.
card.code:

accordion.name: accordion
accordion.title: Accordion
accordion.description: A panel that can be expanded, built on details and summary. CSS component with two classes and no JavaScript.
accordion.intro: The class goes on a `<details>` with a `<summary>` first. The browser handles opening, closing, the keyboard and screen readers announcing "expanded" or "collapsed".
accordion.code:

Anyone who lives in the home and is registered at the address can apply. You must be over 18, or have children of your own living with you.

How long does processing take?

input.name: input
input.title: Input
input.description: A text field for forms, with states for valid and invalid. CSS component.
input.intro: Plain CSS on an ordinary `<input>`, so the browser's own validation, autofill and keyboard handling work as before.
input.code:
<label class="lt-label" for="email">Email address</label>
<input class="lt-input" id="email" type="email" placeholder="alex@example.com" />

<label class="lt-label" for="confirm">Confirm email address</label>
<input class="lt-input" id="confirm" type="email" data-state="success" value="alex@example.com" />

<label class="lt-label" for="backup">Backup email</label>
<input class="lt-input" id="backup" type="email" data-state="invalid" aria-invalid="true" value="alex@" />

<label class="lt-label" for="registered">Registered email address</label>
<input class="lt-input" id="registered" type="email" value="alex@example.com" disabled />

demo.html:
<label class="lt-label" for="email">Email address</label>
<input class="lt-input" id="email" type="email" placeholder="alex@example.com" />

<label class="lt-label" for="confirm">Confirm email address</label>
<input class="lt-input" id="confirm" type="email" data-state="success" value="alex@example.com" />

<label class="lt-label" for="backup">Backup email</label>
<input class="lt-input" id="backup" type="email" data-state="invalid" aria-invalid="true" value="alex@" />

<label class="lt-label" for="registered">Registered email address</label>
<input class="lt-input" id="registered" type="email" value="alex@example.com" disabled />

select.name: select
select.title: Select
select.description: A dropdown list. CSS component with one class and no JavaScript.
select.intro: The same appearance and states as [Input](../input/), on a real `<select>`. The browser's own list is then used, the one that already works with the keyboard, screen readers and the phone's built-in picker.
select.code:
<label class="lt-label" for="country">Country</label>
<select class="lt-select" id="country" name="country">
  <option value="">Choose a country</option>
  <option>Canada</option>
  <option selected>Ireland</option>
  <option>United Kingdom</option>
</select>

<label class="lt-label" for="city">City</label>
<select class="lt-select" id="city" data-state="invalid" aria-invalid="true">
  <option value="" selected>Choose a city</option>
</select>

<label class="lt-label" for="registered">Registered country</label>
<select class="lt-select" id="registered" disabled>
  <option selected>Ireland</option>
</select>

demo.html:
<label class="lt-label" for="country">Country</label>
<select class="lt-select" id="country" name="country">
  <option value="">Choose a country</option>
  <option>Canada</option>

</select>

<select class="lt-select" id="registered" disabled>
  <option selected>Ireland</option>
</select>

checkbox.name: checkbox
checkbox.title: Checkbox
checkbox.description: A checkbox for a choice that stands on its own. CSS component with two classes and no JavaScript.
checkbox.intro: Plain CSS on an ordinary `<input type="checkbox">`, so the keyboard, `FormData` and the browser's own validation work as before. If the user should choose one of several options, [Radio](../radio/) is right. If the choice turns a setting on or off and takes effect at once, use [Switch](../switch/).

radio.name: radio
radio.title: Radio
radio.description: Radio buttons for one choice among several. A CSS component with two classes and no JavaScript.
radio.intro: Plain CSS on an ordinary `<input type="radio">`. The buttons in a group are tied together by `name`, and that is what lets only one be selected, and lets the arrow keys move between them.
radio.code: How do you want to receive the answer?

demo.html: How do you want to receive the answer?

textarea.name: textarea
textarea.title: Textarea
textarea.description: A multi-line text field. A CSS component with one class and no JavaScript.
textarea.intro: The same look and states as [Input](../input/), for answers longer than one line.
textarea.code:
<label class="lt-label" for="reason">Reason</label>
<textarea class="lt-textarea" id="reason" rows="3"
  placeholder="Write a short reason"></textarea>

<label class="lt-label" for="message">Message to the caseworker</label>
<textarea class="lt-textarea" id="message"
  data-state="success">I am moving to a new address on 1 June.</textarea>

<label class="lt-label" for="answer">Detailed answer</label>
<textarea class="lt-textarea" id="answer"
  data-state="invalid" aria-invalid="true">Too short</textarea>

<label class="lt-label" for="note">Note</label>
<textarea class="lt-textarea" id="note"
  disabled>The case is closed and cannot be changed.</textarea>

demo.html:
<label class="lt-label" for="reason">Reason</label>
<textarea class="lt-textarea" id="reason" rows="3"
  placeholder="Write a short reason"></textarea>

<label class="lt-label" for="message">Message to the caseworker</label>

table.name: table
table.title: Table
table.description: A table for data in rows and columns. CSS component with two classes and no JavaScript.
table.intro: The class goes on a real `<table>`. It is `<th>` with `scope` that lets screen readers say "Amount, £1,240" when the user is in a cell. If you build the table from `<div>` elements, that connection does not exist, and the numbers have no meaning.
table.code:
Invoices in 2026
Invoice Due Amount
2026-0481 4 March £1,240
2026-0482 4 April £980

demo.html:
Invoices in 2026
Invoice Due Amount

2026-0482 4 April £980

tooltip.name: tooltip
tooltip.title: Tooltip
tooltip.description: A small help text shown on hover and focus. CSS component with two classes and no JavaScript.
tooltip.intro: A bubble with an addition to something that is already on the screen. It must never carry information the user needs: on a touch screen there is neither hover nor focus until something is tapped.
tooltip.code: The case is moved to the archive and can be brought back

demo.html: The case is moved to the archive and can be brought back

link.name: link
link.title: Link
link.description: Link style for navigation in running text. A CSS component with one class and no JavaScript.
link.intro: A link style with a clear underline, hover and a focus indicator. If the link should look like a button, use [Button](../button/) on the `<a>` element instead.
link.code: Your application has been sent. You will find it under My applications, and we will send you an email when it has been processed.

demo.html: Your application has been sent. You will find it under My applications, and we will send you an email when it has been processed.

avatar.name: avatar
avatar.title: Avatar
avatar.description: Profile picture or initials. A CSS component with two classes and no JavaScript.
avatar.intro: A round surface with a picture or initials. The component says nothing about who the person is: the text next to it does that, or a text you give the picture.
avatar.code: JS JS JS KB

demo.html: JS JS JS KB

divider.name: divider
divider.title: Divider
divider.description: A line between parts of the content. A CSS component with one class and no JavaScript.
divider.intro: The class goes on a plain `<hr>`. The browser's own rule has both a border and a height, and both have to be reset before the colour from the tokens is the only one shown. It also has auto margins at the sides, which in a flex column make the line 0 pixels wide. The class resets them, so the line fills the width.

heading.name: heading
heading.title: Heading
heading.description: Headings in six sizes, independent of level. A CSS component with one class and no JavaScript.
heading.intro: Size and level are two different things. The level is `<h1>` to `<h6>` and decides the structure screen readers navigate by. `data-size` only decides how large the text looks.

label.name: label
label.title: Label
label.description: A label for form fields, with marking of required and optional. A CSS component.
label.intro: The right typography on `<label>`, and one consistent way to mark required and optional fields. If you are setting up a whole field, [Field](../field/) is usually simpler. It sets `for`, `id` and `aria-describedby` for you.
label.code:
<label class="lt-label" for="name">Full name</label>
<input class="lt-input" id="name" type="text" />

<label class="lt-label" data-required="symbol" for="email">Email address</label>
<input class="lt-input" id="email" type="email" required />

<label class="lt-label" data-required="text" for="phone">Phone number</label>
<input class="lt-input" id="phone" type="tel" required />

<label class="lt-label" data-optional="" for="address">Address</label>
<input class="lt-input" id="address" type="text" />

<label class="lt-label" aria-disabled="true" for="org-number">Organisation number</label>
<input class="lt-input" id="org-number" type="text" disabled />

demo.html:
<label class="lt-label" for="name">Full name</label>
<input class="lt-input" id="name" type="text" />

<label class="lt-label" data-required="symbol" for="email">Email address</label>
<input class="lt-input" id="email" type="email" required />

<label class="lt-label" data-required="text" for="phone">Phone number</label>
<input class="lt-input" id="phone" type="tel" required />

<label class="lt-label" data-optional="" for="address">Address</label>
<input class="lt-input" id="address" type="text" />

<label class="lt-label" aria-disabled="true" for="org-number">Organisation number</label>
<input class="lt-input" id="org-number" type="text" disabled />

fieldset.name: fieldset
fieldset.title: Fieldset
fieldset.description: A group of controls with a shared label. CSS component with two classes and no JavaScript.
fieldset.intro: `<fieldset>` with `<legend>` is the one way to give a set of radio buttons or checkboxes a shared label that screen readers announce before each option. A heading above the group looks the same, but is not heard.
fieldset.code: Who are you applying on behalf of?

demo.html: Who are you applying on behalf of?

help-text.name: help-text
help-text.title: Help Text
help-text.description: Explanatory text below a form field. A CSS component with one class and no JavaScript.
help-text.intro: The small text below a field that explains what the system expects. If the text is an error message, use [Error Text](../error-text/).

error-text.name: error-text
error-text.title: Error Text
error-text.description: Error message below a form field. A CSS component with one class and no JavaScript.
error-text.intro: The message shown when a field cannot be submitted as it stands. It belongs right below the field, not at the top of the page. If the text should explain what the field expects before the user has done anything, use [Help Text](../help-text/).
error-text.code:

We cannot find this address in the population register. Check that it is correct.

file-upload.name: file-upload
file-upload.title: File Upload
file-upload.description: A field for uploading files. A CSS component with two classes and no JavaScript.
file-upload.intro: The class goes on a plain `<input type="file">`. The button inside is the browser's own, and its text comes from the operating system's language. It cannot be translated, so the label above the field has to say what to upload.
file-upload.code: PDF or image, up to 10 MB per file.

demo.html: PDF or image, up to 10 MB per file.

search.name: search
search.title: Search
search.description: A search field with a magnifying glass. A CSS component with two classes and no JavaScript.
search.intro: An `lt-input` with room for a magnifying glass. Both classes are set, so every state and variable from [Input](../input/) applies here too.
search.code:
<form class="lt-search-row" role="search">
  <label class="lt-label lt-sr-only" for="search">Search cases</label>
  <input class="lt-input lt-search" type="search" id="search" name="q" placeholder="Search cases" />
  <button class="lt-button" type="submit">Search</button>
</form>

  <label class="lt-label lt-sr-only" for="search">Search cases</label>
  <input class="lt-input lt-search" type="search" id="search" name="q" placeholder="Search cases" />

getting-started.name: getting-started
getting-started.title: Getting started
getting-started.description: Install LO-TEK, import what you need, and get the first component on screen.
getting-started.code:
npm install @lo-tek/interfaces

// main.js or main.ts, at the top
    import "@lo-tek/interfaces/tokens.css"
    import "@lo-tek/interfaces/button.css"

type-safe-use.name: type-safe-use
type-safe-use.title: Type-safe use
type-safe-use.description: One namespace, one shape. Autocompletion for the whole system, without tying you to a framework.
type-safe-use.intro: Classes and data attributes make the components framework-independent, but everything is strings:
type-safe-use.code: import { lt } from "@lo-tek/interfaces" Approved View receipt

accessibility.name: accessibility
accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.description: What LO-TEK handles centrally, what is checked by tests, and what you have to do yourself.
accessibility.intro: LO-TEK promises that accessibility is solved in one place, so each app does not have to solve it again. This page says what the promise covers, and where it ends.
